<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Kudzu (Pflanze)]][[en:Kudzu]][[es:Kudzu]][[fa:کودزو]][[fi:Kudzu]][[id:Kudzu]][[jv:Kudzu]][[ml:കുഡ്സു]][[simple:Kudzu]][[vi:Sắn dây]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Kudzu (Pflanze)]][[en:Kudzu]][[es:Kudzu]][[fa:کودزو]][[fi:Kudzu]][[id:Kudzu]][[jv:Kudzu]][[ml:കുഡ്സു]][[simple:Kudzu]][[vi:Sắn dây]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[de:Kudzu (Pflanze)]][[en:Kudzu]][[es:Kudzu]][[fa:کودزو]][[fi:Kudzu]][[id:Kudzu]][[jv:Kudzu]][[ml:കുഡ്സു]][[simple:Kudzu]][[vi:Sắn dây]] {{Short description| part_of of climbing, coiling, and trailing perennial vine}} {{other uses}} {{redirect|葛|the surname|Ge (surname)}} {{Use dmy dates|date=November 2020}} {{missing information|native ecology (mainly predation)|date=February 2022}} [[File:Kudzu on trees in Atlanta, Georgia.jpg|thumb|300px|Kudzu smothering trees in {{ill|Atlanta|en|Atlanta|WD=Q23556|lt=Atlanta}}, Georgia, US]]
'''Kudzu''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|k|uː|d|z|u|,_|ˈ|k|ʊ|d|-|,_|ˈ|k|ʌ|d|-}}), also called '''Japanese arrowroot''' or '''Chinese arrowroot''',<ref>{{PLANTS|symbol=PUMO|taxon=Pueraria montana (Lour.) Merr.|access-date=7 June 2022}}</ref><ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | ''Pueraria montana'' var. ''lobata'' | 314966 | access-date = 11 December 2017}}</ref> is a group of climbing, coiling, and trailing deciduous perennial vines native to much of {{ill|East Asia|en|East Asia|WD=Q27231|lt=East Asia}}, {{ill|Southeast Asia|en|Southeast Asia|WD=Q11708|lt=Southeast Asia}}, and some Pacific islands.<ref name=GRIN/> It is {{ill|Invasive species|en|Invasive species|WD=Q183368|lt=invasive}} in many parts of the world, primarily {{ill|North America|en|North America|WD=Q49|lt=North America}}.
The vine densely climbs over other plants and trees and grows so rapidly that it smothers and kills them by blocking most of the sunlight and taking root space.<ref name="alabama" /> The plants are in the genus ''{{ill|Pueraria|en|Pueraria|WD=Q133126|lt=Pueraria}}'', in the pea family {{ill|Fabaceae|en|Fabaceae|WD=Q44448|lt=Fabaceae}}, subfamily {{ill|Faboideae|en|Faboideae|WD=Q316856|lt=Faboideae}}. The name is derived from the {{ill|Japanese language|en|Japanese language|WD=Q5287|lt=Japanese}} name for the plant [[:en:East Asian arrowroot|East Asian arrowroot]], (''Pueraria montana'' var. ''lobata''), {{nihongo||クズ/葛|kuzu}}.<ref>{{cite Merriam-Webster|kudzu|access-date=2017-10-05}}</ref>{{refn|group=note| The Japanese character {{lang|ja|葛}} was always rendered as {{lang|ja|くず}} in {{ill|Kana|en|Kana|WD=Q187659|lt=Kana}} (usually {{ill|Romanization of Japanese|en|Romanization of Japanese|WD=Q192509|lt=romanized}} as {{transliteration|ja|kuzu}}) and pronounced {{IPA|ja|kɯzɯ|}}, and the English spelling ''kudzu'' comes from an old {{ill|Hepburn romanization|en|Hepburn romanization|WD=Q667558|lt=Hepburn romanization}}.<ref>{{cite book|title=A Japanese-English And English-Japanese Dictionary|author=James Curtis Hepburn|year=1872|publisher=American Presbyterian mission press|url=http://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=nyp.33433081858254;view=1up;seq=326|pages=277|edition=2nd|access-date=May 14, 2023|archive-date=January 1, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160101221254/http://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=nyp.33433081858254;view=1up;seq=326|url-status=live}}</ref> Another word {{nihongo3|"scrap"|屑}} was rendered as {{nihongo||くづ|kudzu}} and pronounced {{IPA|ja|kɯdzɯ|}}. Both words are now spelled {{lang|ja|くず}} ({{transliteration|ja|kuzu}}), and most speakers of Japanese no longer make the {{ill|Phonemic contrast|en|Phonemic contrast|WD=Q17141239|lt=distinction}} between {{IPA|[zɯ]}} and {{IPA|[dzɯ]}} (a [[:en:phonemic merger|phonemic merger]]), so the two words are {{ill|homonym|en|homonym|WD=Q160843|lt=homonym}}s for them.<ref>{{cite book|last=Vance|first=Timothy J.|year=2008|title=The Sounds of Japanese|publisher=Cambridge University Press|pages=85–6|isbn=978-0-5216-1754-3}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Labrune|first=Laurence|year=2012|title=The Phonology of Japanese|publisher=Oxford University Press|pages=64–5|isbn=978-0-19-954583-4}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.weblio.jp/content/%E3%81%8F%E3%81%9A|title=くず|work=[[Daijirin]]|publisher=[[Weblio]]|access-date=2017-10-05}}</ref>}} Where these plants are {{ill|Naturalisation (biology)|en|Naturalisation (biology)|WD=Q2878495|lt=naturalized}}, they can be invasive and are considered {{ill|noxious weed|en|noxious weed|WD=Q7067310|lt=noxious weed}}s. The plant is edible, but often sprayed with herbicides.<ref name="alabama" />
==Taxonomy== [[File:Kudzu seedpods 6580.JPG|thumb|Kudzu seedpods]]
The name kudzu describes one or more species in the genus ''{{ill|Pueraria|en|Pueraria|WD=Q133126|lt=Pueraria}}'' that are closely related, and some of them are considered to be {{ill|Variety (botany)|en|Variety (botany)|WD=Q767728|lt=varieties}} rather than full species. The morphological differences between the subspecies of ''P. montana'' are subtle; they can breed with each other, and introduced kudzu populations {{ill|Kudzu in the United States|en|Kudzu in the United States|WD=Q6441834|lt=in the United States}} apparently have ancestry from more than one of the subspecies.<ref name="jewett2003">{{Cite journal| title = Characterizing Specimens of Kudzu and Related Taxa with RAPD's | jstor = 4034173 |author1=D. K. Jewett |author2=C. J. Jiang |author3=K. O. Britton |author4=J. H. Sun |author5=J. Tang | journal = Castanea | volume = 68 | issue = 3 |date=1 September 2003| pages = 254–260 | issn = 0008-7475 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1111/j.1365-3180.2005.00462.x | title = Genetic diversity of Pueraria lobata (kudzu) and closely related taxa as revealed by inter-simple sequence repeat analysis | first6 = X-J | last6 = Ge | first5 = W H | last5 = Ye | first4 = K O | last4 = Britton | first3 = D K | last3 = Jewett | first2 = Z-C | year = 2005 | last2 = Li | last1 = Sun | first1 = J H | journal = Weed Research | volume = 45 | page = 255 | issue = 4 | bibcode = 2005WeedR..45..255S }}</ref> They are: * ''{{ill|Pueraria montana|en|Pueraria montana|WD=Q1054489|lt=P. montana}}''<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/search?q=pueraria+montana+chinensis|title=Varieties on The Plant List}}</ref> ** [[Pueraria montana var. chinensis|''Pueraria montana'' var. ''chinensis'']] <small>(Ohwi) Sanjappa & Pradeep</small> (= ''P. chinensis'') ** {{ill|Pueraria montana var. lobata|en|Pueraria montana var. lobata|WD=Q15198502|lt=''Pueraria montana'' var. ''lobata''}} <small>(Willd.) Sanjappa & Pradeep</small> (= ''P. lobata'') ** [[Pueraria montana var. thomsonii|''Pueraria montana'' var. ''thomsonii'']] <small>(Benth.) Wiersema ex D.B. Ward</small> (= ''P. thomsonii'') * ''[[Pueraria edulis|P. edulis]]'' * ''{{ill|Pueraria phaseoloides|en|Pueraria phaseoloides|WD=Q43001987|lt=P. phaseoloides}}'' – proposed to be moved to ''{{ill|Neustanthus|en|Neustanthus|WD=Q43001823|lt=Neustanthus}}''
Various other species in ''Pueraria'' sensu stricto are also known as "kudzu" with an adjective, but they are not as widely cultivated or introduced.
==Ecology== Kudzu has been referred to as "quasi-wild" due to its long history of cultivation, selective breeding into various cultivars, and subsequent return to wild conditions. Some researchers suggest that humans are the main predator of kudzu in its native range, and that human use and cultivation of kudzu both contributes to its success as an invasive species and is a form of biological control for kudzu.<ref name="Zhenyu">{{cite journal |last1=Li |first1=Zhenyu |last2=Dong |first2=Quan |last3=Albright |first3=Thomas |last4=Guo |first4=Qinfeng |title=Natural and human dimensions of a quasi-wild species: The case of kudzu |journal=Biological Invasions |date=2011 |volume=13 |issue=10 |pages=2167–2179|doi=10.1007/s10530-011-0042-7 |bibcode=2011BiInv..13.2167L |s2cid=14948770 }}</ref>
==Propagation== {{More citations needed|section|date=May 2020}}
Kudzu spreads by {{ill|vegetative reproduction|en|vegetative reproduction|WD=Q464666|lt=vegetative reproduction}} via {{ill|stolon|en|stolon|WD=Q633912|lt=stolon}}s (runners) that {{ill|Root|en|Root|WD=Q41500|lt=Root}} at the [[:en:node (botany)|nodes]] to form new plants and by {{ill|rhizome|en|rhizome|WD=Q184208|lt=rhizome}}s.<ref>{{Cite web |last=North Carolina Cooperative Extension |title=Pueraria montana var. lobata |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/pueraria-montana-var-lobata/ |access-date=2022-05-03 |website=Gardener Plant Toolbox}}</ref> Kudzu also spreads by {{ill|Seed|en|Seed|WD=Q40763|lt=Seed}}s, which are contained in pods and mature in the autumn, although this is rare.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Kudzu – New York Invasive Species Information |url=http://nyis.info/invasive_species/kudzu/ |access-date=2022-02-28 |language=en-US}}</ref> One or two viable seeds are produced per cluster of pods. The hard-coated seeds can remain viable for several years, and can successfully germinate only when soil is persistently soggy for 5–7 days, with temperatures above 20 °C (68 °F).<ref>https://cefs.ncsu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2021_03_19_Kudzu.pdf?x77888 Weed Focus: Kudzu NCSU</ref> [[File:Flowering kudzu.jpg|thumb|''{{ill|Pueraria montana|en|Pueraria montana|WD=Q1054489|lt=Pueraria montana}}'' flowers]]
Once germinated, saplings must be kept in a well-drained medium that retains high moisture. During this stage of growth, kudzu must receive as much {{ill|Sunlight|en|Sunlight|WD=Q193788|lt=Sunlight}} as possible.<ref>{{Cite web |title=SPECIES: Pueraria montana var. lobata |url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/database/feis/plants/vine/puemonl/all.html |access-date=2024-06-09 |website=www.fs.usda.gov}}</ref> Kudzu saplings are sensitive to mechanical disturbance and are damaged by chemical fertilizers. They do not tolerate long periods of shade or high water tables. Kudzu is able to withstand environments ranging from sunny to shady upon reaching its mature stage; however, forest edges with greater light availability are optimal.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Forseth |first1=Irwin N. |last2=Innis |first2=Anne F. |date=2004 |title=Kudzu ( Pueraria montana ): History, Physiology, and Ecology Combine to Make a Major Ecosystem Threat |url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/07352680490505150 |journal=Critical Reviews in Plant Sciences |language=en |volume=23 |issue=5 |pages=401–413 |doi=10.1080/07352680490505150 |bibcode=2004CRvPS..23..401F |issn=0735-2689}}</ref>
==Invasive species== [[File:KudzuPlants.JPG|thumb|Kudzu plants near {{ill|Canton, Georgia|en|Canton, Georgia|WD=Q2207351|lt=Canton}}, Georgia]]
Kudzu's environmental and {{ill|Environmental degradation|en|Environmental degradation|WD=Q1334780|lt=ecological damage}} results from its outcompeting other species for a resource. Kudzu competes with native flora for light, and acts to block their access to this vital resource by growing over them and shading them with its leaves. Native plants may then die as a result.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Cain|first1=Michael L.|last2=Bowman|first2=William D.|last3=Hacker|first3=Sally D.|title=Ecology|publisher=Sinauer Associates, Inc.|year=2011|page=246}}</ref>[[File:Kudzu graveyard (40580p).jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|Woodland covered in kudzu, {{ill|Brooklyn|en|Brooklyn|WD=Q18419|lt=Brooklyn}}, NY]]When kudzu invades an ecosystem, it makes the {{ill|Plant litter|en|Plant litter|WD=Q2512035|lt=leaf litter}} more {{ill|Lability|en|Lability|WD=Q2630168|lt=labile}}, thereby lessening the {{ill|carbon sequestration|en|carbon sequestration|WD=Q15305550|lt=carbon sequestration}} ability of the soil. This feeds climate change.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Plant litter chemistry and microbial priming regulate the accrual, composition and stability of soil carbon in invaded ecosystems |first1=Mioko |last1=Tamura |first2=Nishanth |last2=Tharayil |journal=New Phytologist |doi=10.1111/nph.12795 |volume=203 |issue=1 |pages=110–124 |date=July 2014 |pmid=24720813|doi-access= |bibcode=2014NewPh.203..110T }}</ref>
===Americas=== {{See also|Kudzu in the United States}}
Kudzu is an infamous weed in the United States,<ref name="Finch" /> where it can be found in 32 states.<ref name="Crockett" /> It is common along roadsides and other disturbed areas throughout most of the southeast,<ref>{{cite web|title=SPECIES: Pueraria montana var. lobata|url=http://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/vine/puemonl/all.html|publisher=US Forest Service - United States Department of Agriculture|access-date=29 September 2015}}</ref> as far north as rural areas of {{ill|Pulaski County, Illinois|en|Pulaski County, Illinois|WD=Q488475|lt=Pulaski County, Illinois}}. The vine has become a sore point in {{ill|Culture of the Southern United States|en|Culture of the Southern United States|WD=Q5193678|lt=Southern US culture}}. Estimates of its rate of spreading differ wildly; it has been described as spreading at the rate of {{convert|150000|acre|km2|abbr=on}} annually,<ref name="scidai">{{cite web| url= https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2009/07/090719185107.htm | title=Controlling Kudzu With Naturally Occurring Fungus | website=[[ScienceDaily]] | date=20 July 2009 | access-date=2009-07-20}}</ref> although in 2015 the {{ill|United States Forest Service|en|United States Forest Service|WD=Q1891156|lt=United States Forest Service}} estimated the rate to be only {{convert|2,500|acre|km2|abbr=on}} per year.<ref name="Finch">{{cite magazine|author=Bill Finch|title=Legend of the Green Monster|magazine=Smithsonian Magazine|volume= 46|number= 5|date=September 2015|page=19|url=http://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/true-story-kudzu-vine-ate-south-180956325/}}</ref>
A small patch of kudzu was discovered in 2009 in {{ill|Leamington, Ontario|en|Leamington, Ontario|WD=Q2566566|lt=Leamington, Ontario}}, the second-warmest growing region of Canada after south coastal British Columbia.<ref>{{cite web |date=27 September 2009 |title=Kudzu: Invasion of the killer vines or a tempest in a teapot? |url=http://ckdp.ca/kudzu-invasion-of-the-killer-vines-or-a-tempest-in-a-teapot/ |access-date=2010-04-20 |publisher=Chatham-Kent Daily Post}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Wingrove |first=Josh |date=24 September 2009 |title='Vine that ate the South' has landed in the Great White North |newspaper=The Globe and Mail |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/national/vine-that-ate-the-south-has-landed-in-the-great-white-north/article4287178/ |access-date=14 October 2013}}</ref>
Kudzu was introduced from Japan into the United States at the Japanese pavilion in the 1876 {{ill|Centennial Exposition|en|Centennial Exposition|WD=Q984109|lt=Centennial Exposition}} in Philadelphia.<ref name="stewart" /> It was also shown at the {{ill|World's Columbian Exposition|en|World's Columbian Exposition|WD=Q285406|lt=Chicago World's Fair}}.<ref name="Crockett">{{Cite web |last=Crockett Peters |first=Clinton |date=2017-08-29 |title=The Miracle Vine |url=https://www.theawl.com/2017/08/kudzu-the-miracle-vine/ |access-date=2022-05-03 |website=The Awl |language=en}}</ref> It remained a garden plant until the {{ill|Dust Bowl|en|Dust Bowl|WD=Q726501|lt=Dust Bowl}} era (1930s–1940s), when the vine was marketed as a way for farmers to stop {{ill|soil erosion|en|soil erosion|WD=Q889503|lt=soil erosion}}. The new {{ill|Natural Resources Conservation Service|en|Natural Resources Conservation Service|WD=Q6980595|lt=Soil Conservation Service}} grew seventy million kudzu seedlings and paid $8 an acre ({{Inflation|US|8|1940|fmt=eq}}) to anyone who would sow the vine. Road and rail builders planted kudzu to stabilize steep slopes. Farmer and journalist Channing Cope, dubbed "kudzu kid" in a 1949 {{ill|Time (magazine)|en|Time (magazine)|WD=Q43297|lt=''Time''}} profile, popularised it in the South as a fix for eroded soils. He started the Kudzu Club of America, which, by 1943, had 20,000 members. The club aimed to plant {{convert|8|e6acre|km2}} across the South.<ref name="Finch" /> Cultivation peaked at over {{convert|1000000|acre|km2|abbr=on|spell=in}} by 1945.<ref>Kudzu: The Vine that Ate the South; PorterBriggs.com http://porterbriggs.com/the-vine-that-ate-the-south/ {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140608025052/http://porterbriggs.com/the-vine-that-ate-the-south/ |date=8 June 2014 }}</ref> Once Soil Service payments ended, much of the kudzu was destroyed as farmers turned the land over to more profitable uses. The Soil Conservation Service stopped promoting kudzu altogether by the 1950s.<ref name="Finch" />[[File:Photograph of dairy cows grazing on kudzu on the farm of G.A. Herford, Columbia County, Georgia, 1952-1957? - DPLA - b3294bc96a065665a0517370b52f8a6a.jpg|thumb|Dairy cows grazing on kudzu in {{ill|Columbia County, Georgia|en|Columbia County, Georgia|WD=Q115307|lt=Columbia County, Georgia}}, {{Circa|1950s}}]]
Kudzu's ongoing mythos as a mile-a-minute invader is likely due to its visibility coating trees at wooded roadsides, thriving in the sunshine at the forest edge. Despite kudzu's notoriety, {{ill|Privet as an invasive plant|en|Privet as an invasive plant|WD=Q17162668|lt=Asian privet}} and invasive {{ill|Rose|en|Rose|WD=Q34687|lt=Rose}}s have each proved to be greater threats in the United States.<ref name="Finch" /> [[File:La Habana, plantas (1983) 03.jpg|thumb|Almendares Park in {{ill|Havana|en|Havana|WD=Q1563|lt=Havana}}, 1983]]
=== Europe === In Europe, kudzu has been included since 2016 on the {{ill|List of invasive alien species of Union concern|en|List of invasive alien species of Union concern|WD=Q26155727|lt=list of Invasive Alien Species of Union concern}} (the Union list).<ref>{{Cite web|title=List of Invasive Alien Species of Union concern - Environment - European Commission|url=https://ec.europa.eu/environment/nature/invasivealien/list/index_en.htm|access-date=2021-07-27|website=ec.europa.eu}}</ref> This means that this species cannot be imported, cultivated, transported, commercialized, planted, or intentionally released into the environment anywhere in the European Union.<ref>{{Cite web|title=REGULATION (EU) No 1143/2014 of the European parliament and of the council of 22 October 2014 on the prevention and management of the introduction and spread of invasive alien species|url=https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32014R1143&from=EN}}</ref>
There are only some kudzu populations in certain regions of Italy and Switzerland. In Switzerland it occurs almost exclusively in {{ill|Ticino|en|Ticino|WD=Q12724|lt=Ticino}}, where it has been found in the wild since at least 1956.<ref>{{cite web |title=Pueraria lobata (Willd.) Ohwi |url=https://www.infoflora.ch/de/flora/pueraria-lobata.html |website=info flora – National Data and Information Center on the Swiss Flora |access-date=16 July 2023 |format=PDF |date=14 July 2023}}</ref> Most outbreaks are concentrated around {{ill|Lake Lugano|en|Lake Lugano|WD=Q14418|lt=Lake Lugano}} and {{ill|Lake Maggiore|en|Lake Maggiore|WD=Q14379|lt=Lake Maggiore}}, where the climate (hot summers and mild winters) encourages its growth. However, outbreaks in peripheral areas such as the Onsernone Valley and Lower Leventina are likely due to the illegal disposal of plant waste. A plan is currently in place to reduce and eventually eradicate the kudzu population in Ticino.<ref name=wwnet_moretti>{{cite web |last=Moretti |first=Giorgio |title=Kudzu: where to from here? |url=https://www.waldwissen.net/en/forestry/forest-protection/invasive-species/kudzu-where-to-from-here |website=waldwissen.net |access-date=16 July 2023 |date=12 December 2021}}</ref>
===Other regions=== During {{ill|Pacific War|en|Pacific War|WD=Q184425|lt=Pacific War}}, kudzu was introduced to {{ill|Vanuatu|en|Vanuatu|WD=Q686|lt=Vanuatu}} and {{ill|Fiji|en|Fiji|WD=Q712|lt=Fiji}} by {{ill|United States Armed Forces|en|United States Armed Forces|WD=Q11211|lt=United States Armed Forces}} to serve as {{ill|Military camouflage|en|Military camouflage|WD=Q196086|lt=camouflage}} for equipment and has become a major weed.<ref>{{cite book|last=Walker|first=Timothy|title=Plant Conservation: Why it matters and how it works|year=2013|publisher=Timber Press|isbn=978-1604692600|page=157}}</ref>
Kudzu is also becoming a problem in {{ill|Queensland|en|Queensland|WD=Q36074|lt=northeastern Australia}}.<ref>{{Cite journal | doi=10.1111/epp.12172|title = Ecology and distribution of the Southeast Asian invasive liana Kudzu, Pueraria lobata (Fabaceae), in Southern Switzerland| journal=EPPO Bulletin| volume=44| issue=3| pages=490–501|year = 2014|last1 = Gigon|first1 = A.| last2=Pron| first2=S.| last3=Buholzer| first3=S.}}</ref>
In {{ill|New Zealand|en|New Zealand|WD=Q664|lt=New Zealand}}, kudzu was declared an "unwanted organism" and was added to the Biosecurity New Zealand register in 2002.<ref>{{cite journal|date=1 August 2002|title=Kudzu vine an unwanted organism|journal=Biosecurity|issue=37|issn=1174-4618|url=http://planet.botany.uwc.ac.za/nisl/Biosecurity/biosecurity-37.pdf|last=Gill|first=George|access-date=6 June 2017|archive-date=10 December 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171210020152/http://planet.botany.uwc.ac.za/nisl/Biosecurity/biosecurity-37.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>
==Control==
===Crown removal=== Destroying the full underground system, which can be extremely large and deep, is not necessary for successful long-term control of kudzu. Killing or removing the kudzu {{ill|root crown|en|root crown|WD=Q2983009|lt=root crown}}<ref name="kokudzu">{{cite web|url=http://www.kokudzu.com/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070917144730/http://www.kokudzu.com/ |archive-date=2007-09-17 |title=Kudzu Control Without Chemicals|access-date=20 July 2022|publisher=kokudzu.com|year=2007}}</ref> and all rooting runners is sufficient. The root crown is a fibrous knob of tissue that sits on top of the roots. Crowns form from multiple vine nodes that root to the ground, and range from pea- to basketball-sized.<ref name="kokudzu" /> These crowns and attached tuberous roots can weigh 400 or 500 pounds (180 to 225 kilograms) and extend up to twenty feet (six meters) into the ground.<ref>Diane Hoots and Juanita Baldwin, "Kudsu - The Vine to Love or Hate, Kodak, Tennessee, Suntop press, (1996) Page 5</ref> The age of the crowns is correlated to how deep they are in the ground. Nodes and crowns are the source of all kudzu vines, and roots cannot produce vines. If any portion of a root crown remains after attempted removal, the kudzu plant may still grow back.
Mechanical methods of control involve cutting off crowns from roots, usually just below ground level. This immediately kills the plant. Cutting off the above-ground vines is not sufficient for an immediate kill. Destroying all removed crown material is necessary. Buried crowns can regenerate into healthy kudzu. Transporting crowns in soil removed from a kudzu infestation is one common way that kudzu unexpectedly spreads and shows up in new locations.
Close mowing every week, regular heavy {{ill|grazing|en|grazing|WD=Q3239189|lt=grazing}} for many successive years, or repeated {{ill|Tillage|en|Tillage|WD=Q878333|lt=cultivation}} may be effective, as this serves to deplete root reserves.<ref name="kokudzu" /> If done in the spring, cutting off vines must be repeated. Regrowth appears to exhaust the plant's stored {{ill|Carbohydrate|en|Carbohydrate|WD=Q11358|lt=Carbohydrate}} reserves. Harvested kudzu can be fed to livestock, burned, or composted.
In the United States, the city of {{ill|Chattanooga, Tennessee|en|Chattanooga, Tennessee|WD=Q186702|lt=Chattanooga, Tennessee}} undertook a trial program in 2010 using {{ill|Goat|en|Goat|WD=Q2934|lt=Goat}}s and {{ill|llama|en|llama|WD=Q42569|lt=llama}}s to graze on the plant. Similar efforts to reduce widespread nuisance kudzu growth have also been undertaken in the cities of {{ill|Winston-Salem, North Carolina|en|Winston-Salem, North Carolina|WD=Q49227|lt=Winston-Salem, North Carolina}}<ref name="WXII12.com">{{cite web|url= http://www.wxii12.com/news/24828912/detail.html|title= Winston-Salem Using Goats To Attack Problem Kudzu Vines|access-date= 2010-09-08|publisher= Wxii12.com|date= 2010-08-31|first= Betsy|last= Bramlett|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120306092331/http://www.wxii12.com/news/24828912/detail.html|archive-date=2012-03-06}}</ref> and {{ill|Tallahassee, Florida|en|Tallahassee, Florida|WD=Q37043|lt=Tallahassee, Florida}}.<ref>{{cite web|last=Neofotis|first=Peter|title= Kudzu (Pueraria montana)|url=http://www.columbia.edu/itc/cerc/danoff-burg/invasion_bio/inv_spp_summ/Pueraria_montana.html|work=Introduced Species Summary Project|publisher=Columbia University|access-date=17 September 2011}}</ref>
[[:en:Prescribed burning|Prescribed burning]] is used on old extensive infestations to remove vegetative cover and promote seed germination for removal or treatment. While fire is not an effective way to kill kudzu,<ref name="kokudzu" /> equipment, such as a [[:en:skid loader|skid loader]], can later remove crowns and kill kudzu with minimal disturbance or erosion of soil.<ref name="washington">{{cite web|url=http://www.nwcb.wa.gov/weed_info/Pueraria_lobata.html|title=Written Findings of the State Noxious Weed Control Board|access-date=20 August 2007|publisher=Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board|year=2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927090123/http://www.nwcb.wa.gov/weed_info/Pueraria_lobata.html|archive-date=27 September 2011}}</ref>
===Herbicide=== A systemic {{ill|herbicide|en|herbicide|WD=Q178266|lt=herbicide}}, for example, {{ill|glyphosate|en|glyphosate|WD=Q407232|lt=glyphosate}},<ref name=SE>{{Cite web|url=http://www.se-eppc.org/manual/kudzu.html|title=Southeast Exotic Pest Plant Council Invasive Plant Manual}}</ref> {{ill|triclopyr|en|triclopyr|WD=Q2303660|lt=triclopyr}},<ref name=SE /> or {{ill|picloram|en|picloram|WD=Q424662|lt=picloram}},<ref name=MDC>{{Cite web|url=http://mdc.mo.gov/landwater-care/plant-management/invasive-plant-management/kudzu|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110526102822/http://mdc.mo.gov/landwater-care/plant-management/invasive-plant-management/kudzu|url-status=dead|title=Missouri Department of Conservation - Kudzu|archivedate=26 May 2011}}</ref> can be applied directly on cut stems, which is an effective means of transporting the herbicide into the kudzu's extensive root system.<ref name=NPS>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nps.gov/plants/alien/fact/pumo1.htm|title=National Park Service - Kudzu}}</ref> Herbicides can be used after other methods of control, such as mowing, grazing, or burning, which can allow for an easier application of the chemical to the weakened plants.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.bugwood.org/crp/kudzu.html |title=Bugwood Network (Center for Invasive Species and Ecosystem Health) |access-date=27 November 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130308055202/http://www.bugwood.org/crp/kudzu.html |archive-date=8 March 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref> In large-scale forestry infestations, soil-active herbicides have been shown to be highly effective.<ref name=NPS />
After initial herbicidal treatment, follow-up treatments and monitoring are usually necessary, depending on how long the kudzu has been growing in an area. Up to 10 years of supervision may be needed after the initial chemical placement to make sure the plant does not return.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kokudzu.com/Shared/PDF/HerbicideTreatmentsForKudzu.pdf|author=Matt Nespeca|date=August 2007|publisher=kokudzu.com|title=Kudzu Control Methods and Strategies|access-date=6 June 2017|archive-date=25 June 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160625080857/http://kokudzu.com/Shared/PDF/HerbicideTreatmentsForKudzu.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>
===Fungi=== Since 1998, the United States' {{ill|Agricultural Research Service|en|Agricultural Research Service|WD=Q2827151|lt=Agricultural Research Service}} has experimented with using the fungus ''{{ill|Myrothecium verrucaria|en|Myrothecium verrucaria|WD=Q6948523|lt=Myrothecium verrucaria}}'' as a biologically based herbicide against kudzu.<ref name="scidai" /> A {{ill|diacetylverrucarol|en|diacetylverrucarol|WD=Q5270219|lt=diacetylverrucarol}} spray based on ''M. verrucaria'' works under a variety of conditions (including the absence of {{ill|dew|en|dew|WD=Q41097|lt=dew}}), causes minimal injury to many of the other woody plants in kudzu-infested habitats, and takes effect quickly enough that kudzu treated with it in the morning starts showing evidence of damage by midafternoon.<ref name="scidai"/> Initial formulations of the herbicide produced toxic levels of other {{ill|trichothecene|en|trichothecene|WD=Q257954|lt=trichothecene}}s as byproducts, though the ARS discovered that growing ''M. verrucaria'' in a [[:en:fermenter|fermenter]] on a liquid diet (instead of a solid) limited or eliminated the problem.<ref name="scidai"/>
==Uses==
===Soil improvement and preservation=== Kudzu has been used as a form of {{ill|erosion control|en|erosion control|WD=Q5395394|lt=erosion control}} and to enhance the soil. As a {{ill|legume|en|legume|WD=Q145909|lt=legume}}, it increases the {{ill|nitrogen|en|nitrogen|WD=Q627|lt=nitrogen}} in the soil by a symbiotic relationship with {{ill|Nitrogen fixation|en|Nitrogen fixation|WD=Q272467|lt=nitrogen-fixing}} {{ill|Bacteria|en|Bacteria|WD=Q10876|lt=Bacteria}}.<ref name="appalachia">{{cite web|url=http://www.a-spi.org/tp/tp55.htm|title=Kudzu in Appalachia|access-date=20 August 2007|publisher=Appalachia -- Science in the Public Interest|year=2000|author=Amanda Allen|work=ASPI Technical Series TP 55|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928071603/http://www.a-spi.org/tp/tp55.htm|archive-date=28 September 2007}}</ref> Its deep taproots also transfer valuable minerals from the {{ill|subsoil|en|subsoil|WD=Q681004|lt=subsoil}} to the topsoil, thereby improving the topsoil. In the deforested section of the central [[:en:Amazon Basin|Amazon Basin]] in {{ill|Brazil|en|Brazil|WD=Q155|lt=Brazil}}, it has been used for improving the soil pore-space in clay {{ill|latosol|en|latosol|WD=Q6496924|lt=latosol}}s, thus freeing even more water for plants than in the soil prior to deforestation.<ref name="brazil">{{cite journal|title=Changes in soil pore-space distribution following deforestation and revegetation: An example from the Central Amazon Basin, Brazil |year=1991|author1=Chauvel, A |author2=Grimaldi, M |author3=Tessier, D |journal=Forest Ecology and Management |doi=10.1016/0378-1127(91)90147-N |volume=38 |issue=3–4 |pages=259–271|bibcode=1991ForEM..38..259C |url=http://horizon.documentation.ird.fr/exl-doc/pleins_textes/divers16-03/38584.pdf }}</ref>
===Animal feed=== Kudzu can be used by grazing animals, as it is high in quality as a {{ill|Fodder|en|Fodder|WD=Q211439|lt=forage}} and palatable to [[livestock]]. It can be grazed until {{ill|frost|en|frost|WD=Q4590598|lt=frost}} and even slightly after. Kudzu had been used in the southern United States specifically to feed goats on land that had limited resources. Kudzu {{ill|hay|en|hay|WD=Q336989|lt=hay}} typically has a 22–23% crude protein content and over 60% total digestible nutrient value. The quality of the leaves decreases as {{ill|vine|en|vine|WD=Q917284|lt=vine}} content increases relative to the {{ill|Leaf|en|Leaf|WD=Q33971|lt=Leaf}} content. Kudzu also has low forage yields despite its rate of {{ill|cell growth|en|cell growth|WD=Q189159|lt=growth}}, yielding around two to four tons of dry matter per acre annually. It is also difficult to bale due to its vining growth and its slowness in shedding water. This makes it necessary to place kudzu hay under sheltered protection after being baled. Fresh kudzu is readily consumed by all types of grazing animals, but frequent grazing over three to four years can ruin even established stands. Thus, kudzu only serves well as a grazing crop on a temporary basis.<ref name="alabama">{{cite web|url=http://www.aces.edu/pubs/docs/A/ANR-0065/|title=Kudzu in Alabama: History, Uses, and Control|access-date=20 August 2007|publisher=Alabama Cooperative Extension System|year=1999|author1=John Everest |author2=James Miller |author3=Donald Ball |author4=Mike Patterson|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120616073734/http://www.aces.edu/pubs/docs/A/ANR-0065/|archive-date=16 June 2012 }}</ref>
===Basketry=== Kudzu fiber has long been used for fiber art and basketry. The long runners which propagate the kudzu fields and the larger vines which cover trees make excellent weaving material. Some basketmakers use the material green. Others use it after splitting it in half, allowing it to dry and then rehydrating it using hot water. Both traditional and contemporary basketry artists use kudzu.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jSQzR6_h9yEC&q=kudzu+basket|title=The book of kudzu: a culinary & healing guide|author1=[[William Shurtleff]] |author2=[[Akiko Aoyagi]] |publisher=Soyinfo Center|year=1977|isbn=9780394420684}}</ref> [[File:Kudzu basket hen.jpg|alt=A basket with a large vine and its tendrils incorporated into the weave|thumb|Appalachian hen basket, {{Circa|2011}}]]
===Phytochemicals and uses=== Kudzu contains {{ill|isoflavone|en|isoflavone|WD=Q412519|lt=isoflavone}}s, including {{ill|puerarin|en|puerarin|WD=Q4392082|lt=puerarin}} (about 60% of the total isoflavones), {{ill|daidzein|en|daidzein|WD=Q408732|lt=daidzein}}, {{ill|daidzin|en|daidzin|WD=Q3814656|lt=daidzin}} (structurally related to {{ill|genistein|en|genistein|WD=Q415957|lt=genistein}}), {{ill|mirificin|en|mirificin|WD=Q27158378|lt=mirificin}}, and [[:en:salvianolic acid|salvianolic acid]], among numerous others identified.<ref name="mol">{{cite journal|pmid=28353641|pmc=6154678|year=2017|last1=Wang|first1=F. R.|title=Rapid Determination of 30 Polyphenols in Tongmai Formula, a Combination of Puerariae Lobatae Radix, Salviae Miltiorrhizae Radix et Rhizoma, and Chuanxiong Rhizoma, via Liquid Chromatography-Tandem Mass Spectrometry|journal=Molecules|volume=22|issue=4|pages=545|last2=Zhang|first2=Y|last3=Yang|first3=X. B.|last4=Liu|first4=C. X.|last5=Yang|first5=X. W.|last6=Xu|first6=W|last7=Liu|first7=J. X.|doi=10.3390/molecules22040545|doi-access=free}}</ref> In {{ill|Traditional Chinese medicine|en|Traditional Chinese medicine|WD=Q200253|lt=Traditional Chinese medicine}}, where it is known as ''gé gēn'' (gegen), kudzu is considered one of the [[:en:50 Fundamental Herbs|50 fundamental herbs]] thought to have therapeutic effects, although there is no high-quality {{ill|clinical research|en|clinical research|WD=Q5133849|lt=clinical research}} to indicate it has any activity or therapeutic use in humans.<ref name="drugs">{{cite web|url=https://www.drugs.com/npc/kudzu.html|title=Kudzu|publisher=Drugs.com|date=2017|access-date=28 June 2017}}</ref><ref name="msk">{{cite web|url=https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/kudzu|title=Kudzu|publisher=Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center|date=2017|access-date=28 June 2017}}</ref>{{Refn|See, however, Zhang, Y., Kong, W. N., & Chai, X. Q. (2018).|group=note}} Compounds of {{ill|icariin|en|icariin|WD=Q5985057|lt=icariin}}, astragalus, and {{ill|puerarin|en|puerarin|WD=Q4392082|lt=puerarin}} mitigates iron overload in the cerebral cortex of mice with Alzheimer's disease.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=Yu |last2=Kong |first2=Wei-Na |last3=Chai |first3=Xi-Qing |date=Apr 2018 |title=Compound of icariin, astragalus, and puerarin mitigates iron overload in the cerebral cortex of Alzheimer's disease mice |journal=Neural Regeneration Research |language=en-US |volume=13 |issue=4 |pages=731–736 |doi=10.4103/1673-5374.230302 |pmid=29722328 |pmc=5950686 |s2cid=19158410 |issn=1673-5374 |doi-access=free }}</ref> {{ill|Adverse effect|en|Adverse effect|WD=Q2047938|lt=Adverse effect}}s may occur if kudzu is taken by people with hormone-sensitive cancer or those taking {{ill|tamoxifen|en|tamoxifen|WD=Q412178|lt=tamoxifen}}, antidiabetic medications, or {{ill|methotrexate|en|methotrexate|WD=Q422232|lt=methotrexate}}.<ref name=msk/>[[File:KudzuLeaves.JPG|thumb|Kudzu leaves near {{ill|Canton, Georgia|en|Canton, Georgia|WD=Q2207351|lt=Canton, Georgia}}]]
===Food=== [[:en:kuzuko|The roots]] contain {{ill|Starch|en|Starch|WD=Q41534|lt=Starch}}, which has traditionally been used as a food ingredient in East and Southeast Asia. In {{ill|Vietnam|en|Vietnam|WD=Q881|lt=Vietnam}}, the starch, called ''bột sắn dây'', is flavoured with {{ill|pomelo|en|pomelo|WD=Q80024|lt=pomelo}} oil and then used as a drink in the summer. In {{ill|Korea|en|Korea|WD=Q18097|lt=Korea}}, the plant root is made into {{ill|arrowroot tea|en|arrowroot tea|WD=Q6449330|lt=''chikcha''}} (칡차; "arrowroot tea"), used in traditional medicine, and processed starch used for culinary purposes such as primary ingredient for {{ill|naengmyeon|en|naengmyeon|WD=Q715084|lt=naengmyeon}} (칡냉면). In {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan}}, the plant is known as ''kuzu'' and the starch named ''[[:en:kuzuko|kuzuko]]''. ''Kuzuko'' is used in dishes including ''{{ill|Kuzumochi|en|Kuzumochi|WD=Q6449309|lt=Kuzumochi}}, mizu {{ill|Manjū|en|Manjū|WD=Q599548|lt=Manjū}}'', and ''[[:en:kuzuyu|kuzuyu]]''. It also serves as a thickener for sauces, and can substitute for cornstarch.<ref name="ShurtleffAoyagi1977">{{cite book|last1=Shurtleff|first1=William|last2=Aoyagi|first2=Akiko|title=The Book of Kudzu: A Culinary & Healing Guide|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jSQzR6_h9yEC|year=1977|publisher=Soyinfo Center|isbn=978-0-394-42068-4|page=9}}</ref> [[File:2010 Kuzumochi(Kudzu starch cake) by Sanda-Minoya.jpg|alt=a translucent jelly with black soybeans visible inside|thumb|''{{ill|Kuzumochi|en|Kuzumochi|WD=Q6449309|lt=Kuzumochi}}'', a Japanese pudding]] The flowers are used to make a {{ill|Fruit preserves|en|Fruit preserves|WD=Q74048276|lt=jelly}} that tastes similar to grape jelly.<ref name="Burney" /><ref name="connoisseur">{{cite book |last1=Marchese |first1=C. Marina |title=The Honey Connoisseur |last2=Flottum |first2=Kim |publisher=Black Dog & Leventhal |year=2013 |isbn=9781603763325 |pages=84–85}}</ref> Roots, flowers, and leaves of kudzu show antioxidant activity that suggests food uses.<ref name="Burney">{{cite web|url=http://sun.library.msstate.edu/ETD-db/theses/available/etd-03292010-130857/|title=Determination of antioxidant and total phenolic content of ''Pueraria lobata'' and evaluation of novel food products containing kudzu|author=Sandra Lynn Burney|year=2010|publisher=Mississippi State University|access-date=28 November 2011|archive-date=16 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200616034230/http://sun.library.msstate.edu/ETD-db/theses/available/etd-03292010-130857/|url-status=dead}}</ref> Nearby bee colonies may forage on kudzu nectar during droughts as a last resort, producing a low-viscosity red or purple {{ill|honey|en|honey|WD=Q10987|lt=honey}} that tastes of grape jelly or {{ill|Bubble gum|en|Bubble gum|WD=Q1318753|lt=bubblegum}}.<ref name="connoisseur" />
===Folk medicine=== Kudzu has also been used for centuries in East Asia as {{ill|Traditional medicine|en|Traditional medicine|WD=Q771035|lt=folk medicine}} using {{ill|Herbal tea|en|Herbal tea|WD=Q379932|lt=Herbal tea}}s and {{ill|tincture|en|tincture|WD=Q969804|lt=tincture}}s.<ref name="stewart">{{cite magazine|magazine=Smithsonian Magazine|url=http://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/kudzu-love-it-or-run-68095358/|title= Kudzu: Love It or Run|date = 30 September 2000|author=Doug Stewart|accessdate=21 June 2021}}</ref> Kudzu powder is used in Japan to make an herbal tea called ''[[:en:kuzuyu|kuzuyu]]''. Kakkonto ({{cjkv|c=葛根湯|p=gégēntāng|j=葛根湯|r=kakkontō|l=Kudzu Root Soup}}) is a herbal drink with its origin in {{ill|Traditional Chinese medicine|en|Traditional Chinese medicine|WD=Q200253|lt=Traditional Chinese medicine}}, intended for people having various mild illnesses, such as {{ill|headache|en|headache|WD=Q86|lt=headache}}.<ref name=stewart/>
===Fiber=== Kudzu fiber, known as ko-hemp,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/ko-hemp|title=Definition of KO-HEMP|website=Merriam-Webster}}</ref> is used traditionally to make clothing and paper,<ref>{{Cite journal| title = Kudzu (''Pueraria lobata'' (Willd.) Ohwi) | author = Larry W. Mitich | journal = Weed Technology | volume = 14 | issue = 1 | date = Jan–Mar 2000 | pages = 231–235 | doi = 10.1614/0890-037X(2000)014[0231:KPLWO]2.0.CO;2 | jstor = 3988532 | s2cid = 86120103 }}</ref> and has also been investigated for industrial-scale use.<ref>{{Cite journal| title = Kudzu (Pueraria Lobata): Potential agricultural and industrial resource | journal = Economic Botany | issn = 1874-9364 | volume = 33 | issue = 4 |date = October 1979| doi = 10.1007/BF02858336 | pages = 400–412 |author1=Robert D. Tanner |author2=S. Shahid Hussain |author3=Lindsey A. Hamilton |author4=Frederick T. Wolf | bibcode = 1979EcBot..33..400T | s2cid = 2680987 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal| title = The effect of fermentation (retting) time and harvest time on kudzu (''Pueraria lobata'') fiber strength | journal = Applied Biochemistry and Biotechnology | issn = 1559-0291 | volume = 57–58 | issue = 1 | date = March 1996 | doi = 10.1007/BF02941690 | pages = 75–84 |author1=Sibel Uludag |author2=Veara Loha |author3=Ales Prokop |author4=Robert D. Tanner | s2cid = 189908496 }}</ref> Kudzu fiber is a [[:en:Bast fiber|Bast fiber]] similar to hemp or linen, and has been used for clothing in China for at least 6,000 years and in Japan for at least 1,500 years. In ancient China, kudzu was one of three main clothing and textile materials, with silk and ramie being the other two.<ref name="Zhenyu"/> Kudzu is still currently used in Japan, primarily used to weave {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Obi (sash)|en|Obi (sash)|WD=Q825501|lt=obi}}}} worn in the summer.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.motoji.co.jp/blogs/artists-origins/kudzufu | title=静岡県・葛布（くずふ） }}</ref>
===Other uses=== It may become a valuable asset for the production of {{ill|cellulosic ethanol|en|cellulosic ethanol|WD=Q1053121|lt=cellulosic ethanol}}.<ref>Richard G. Lugar, R. James Woolsey. The New Petroleum. Foreign Affairs. 1999. Vol. 78, No 1. p. 88.</ref> In the {{ill|Southern United States|en|Southern United States|WD=Q49042|lt=Southern United States}}, kudzu is used to make {{ill|Soap|en|Soap|WD=Q34396|lt=Soap}}s, {{ill|lotion|en|lotion|WD=Q1871151|lt=lotion}}s, and {{ill|compost|en|compost|WD=Q212254|lt=compost}}.<ref name="basket">{{cite web|url=http://www.dukeemployees.com/offthewall2.shtml|title=If You Can't Beat Kudzu, Join It|access-date=20 August 2007|publisher=Duke Energy Employee Advocate|year=2003|author=Jeffrey Collins|work=Off the Wall}}</ref>
